notes.meaning: Four rulers from the east formed an alliance to make war against five kings of the Jordan Valley. Chedorlaomer of Elam was the leader of the eastern group, while the western kings ruled cities like Sodom and Gomorrah. This report shows how smaller city-states often banded together under powerful leaders in the ancient world.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historical-critical scholars question whether this campaign took place as described, noting that ancient royal inscriptions do not clearly mention these specific kings or their invasion.

notes.meaning: The five western kings gathered their armies together in the Valley of Siddim, which later became part of the Dead Sea. Before God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, this region was a fertile and populated valley.
The five cities had paid tribute money and served Chedorlaomer for twelve years. In the thirteenth year, they refused to submit any longer and broke away from his rule.

Chedorlaomer and his allies marched down the east side of the Jordan to punish the rebels and crushed several powerful groups along the way, including the Rephaites, Horites, and Amalekites. They swept south through the desert border before turning back north toward the five rebellious cities. Their sweep cut off outside help and showed how powerful the eastern alliance was.

The five local rulers marched out together into the Valley of Siddim to stop the invaders. Even though five armies faced four, the battle pitted small city rulers against a hardened imperial alliance.

The battlefield was covered with sticky tar pits, which made it hard for the local armies to fight or escape. When the armies of Sodom and Gomorrah were beaten, some soldiers fell into these asphalt pits while the rest scrambled to safety in the hills.

The victorious eastern kings entered Sodom and Gomorrah and carried away all the food, livestock, and riches. Having plundered the towns to recover unpaid tribute, the armies began their journey home.

The invaders also captured Abram's nephew Lot and took all his belongings, because Lot had chosen to live inside Sodom. Choosing to dwell among a wicked people put Lot in harm's way when judgment and war arrived.

A survivor of the battle escaped and brought the news to Abram, who is called the Hebrew. Abram was living peacefully near Hebron and had entered into a defense pact with three local Amorite brothers: Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner.

As soon as Abram heard that his kinsman was a prisoner, he gathered 318 dependable, trained men born in his own household. Together with his allies, he chased the invading kings about 150 miles north toward Dan.

Abram launched a surprise night attack by dividing his men into groups to strike the enemy camp from several directions at once. The confusion caused a panic, routing Chedorlaomer's forces, and Abram chased them past Damascus.
Abram recovered everything that had been stolen, including the goods, the captured women, and the other prisoners of war. Above all, he brought back his nephew Lot alive and safely restored.

After Abram returned from defeating the four kings, the king of Sodom came out to meet him in the King's Valley near Jerusalem. The meeting was arranged to celebrate the rescue of the captives and to settle what would happen to the recovered spoil.

Melchizedek, whose name means king of righteousness, ruled over Salem, the ancient city of Jerusalem. He served as a priest of the true God and brought out bread and wine to refresh Abram and his weary men.

differ.view: Melchizedek was a historical, human king-priest whose lack of recorded genealogy served as a prophetic picture of Jesus Christ.
Melchizedek may have been a Christophany, an appearance of the Son of God taking human form before his birth in Bethlehem.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Melchizedek's offering of bread and wine is understood as a sacrifice that directly prefigures the sacrament of the Eucharist.

notes.meaning: Melchizedek pronounced a blessing on Abram in the name of God Most High, who created and owns everything in heaven and earth. By giving this blessing, Melchizedek acted in his official role as God's priest toward Abram.

Melchizedek praised God for handing Abram victory over his enemies, and Abram responded by giving the priest a tenth of all the war spoils. This tithe was an act of worship honoring God as the true giver of the victory.

differ.view: Because Abram gave a tenth before the Mosaic Law was given, giving a tenth remains an enduring standard for Christian financial giving today.
Abram's gift of war spoils was a one-time demonstration of Melchizedek's higher rank, so the New Testament calls believers to generous, proportionate giving rather than a required ten percent.

notes.meaning: The king of Sodom told Abram to return the rescued people to him and keep all the recaptured property as his own reward. By the customs of ancient warfare, Abram had a lawful right to keep all the recovered plunder.

Abram refused the offer, explaining that he had sworn a solemn oath to the Lord, God Most High. He would not keep even a sandal strap from Sodom so that no pagan king could ever claim he had made Abram rich. Abram trusted God alone to supply his needs and fulfill his promises.

Abram accepted only the food his men had already eaten during the pursuit, and he made sure his Amorite allies received their rightful share of the spoil. While he chose strict personal devotion for himself, he did not force his personal vow on his neighbors.
